titre: The 80/20 Attributed to Pareto: 80% of the Land for 20% of Italians
accroche: In 1896, an Italian economist describes a highly unequal distribution of wealth. He will be credited with the 80/20 rule, which an engineer will generalize later.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1896, the Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto, who has held the chair of political economy at the University of Lausanne since 1893, publishes the first volume of his *Cours d'économie politique* (Course in Political Economy). In it he describes a highly unequal distribution of wealth and draws from it a mathematical law of distribution, which he believes holds in every society, in every age and in every country, without giving it the name it bears today. A widespread account credits him with a more striking observation: about 80% of the land of the Kingdom of Italy supposedly belonged to only 20% of the population. Yet this figure remains hard to locate in his work: the versions disagree on the date and even on the country, as the researcher William H. Press, of the University of Texas at Austin, points out in 2025. In 1906, while still teaching in Lausanne, Pareto publishes his *Manuale di economia politica* (Manual of Political Economy), never suspecting that his name will designate, a few decades later, one of the most cited shortcuts in the world of management.

## From an Economic Observation to a Universal Principle

Pareto's idea remains confined to economics for more than forty years. It is the Romanian-born engineer, naturalized American, Joseph Juran who gives it its current reach: in 1941, while working on questions of industrial quality, Juran comes across Pareto's work. In quality problems, a small minority of causes produces the great majority of defects. Juran generalizes Pareto's observation to this industrial finding, and coins a formula that remains famous to sum it up: “the vital few and the trivial many.” The 80/20 principle becomes a quality management tool, then a shortcut applied well beyond: sales, software, customer service.

## A Proportion, Not a Law of Nature

The main risk of the Pareto principle is not that it is false. It is that it is taken literally. The numbers 80 and 20 are neither fixed nor universal, and vary greatly depending on the field observed. The proportion attributed to Pareto does not escape this vagueness: its date and its country vary from one account to another. Juran applied to industrial quality a simple approximation: about 80% of problems stem from 20% of causes. What Pareto and Juran brought to light is therefore not a fixed number. It is a more general and more disturbing observation: in a surprising number of systems, most of the effect comes from a small part of the causes, and the rest, the great majority, weighs almost nothing.

repere.texte: A widely repeated account credits Vilfredo Pareto, author of the Cours d'économie politique (1896-1897), with observing that about 80% of the land of the Kingdom of Italy belonged to only 20% of the population, the proportion that Joseph Juran will generalize in 1941 to industrial quality management.

carte.punch: Pareto is credited with this finding: 80% of Italy's land owned by 20% of the people.
carte.idee: Pareto is credited with observing that about 80% of Italian land belonged to 20% of the population. In 1941, Joseph Juran extends this proportion to quality: “the vital few and the trivial many.” The numbers 80 and 20 vary by field.

quiz.question: What observation is commonly attributed to Vilfredo Pareto, author of the Cours d'économie politique (1896)?
choix: That a small share of the Italian population owned the great majority of the country's land
That 80% of Italian companies of his time went bankrupt within the first five years
That 20% of the laws passed in Italy concentrated 80% of the state's tax revenue
That wealth was distributed perfectly evenly among the twenty Italian regions
quiz.explication: A widespread account credits Pareto with finding a highly unequal distribution of land in Italy, about 80% belonging to 20% of the population, even though this figure remains hard to locate in his work. It is neither an observation about bankruptcies nor about taxation: it is Juran, in 1941, who will generalize this proportion to other fields.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who generalizes Pareto's observation to industrial quality management, and in what year?
choix: The Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto himself, in 1906
The Romanian-born engineer, naturalized American, Joseph Juran, in 1941
The British statistician Ronald Fisher, in 1925
The Austrian economist Joseph Schumpeter, in 1934
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry specifies that it is the Romanian-born engineer, naturalized American, Joseph Juran who, in 1941, while working on questions of industrial quality, generalizes Pareto's observation beyond economics.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What formula does Joseph Juran coin to sum up his generalization of the Pareto principle?
choix: The vital few and the trivial many
Chance never plays dice with the economy
Not everything that counts can always be counted
Quality has no price, but it has a cost
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry quotes Juran's famous formula, “the vital few and the trivial many,” to sum up his generalization of the Pareto principle to quality management.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the entry say about the numbers 80 and 20 themselves?
choix: They have never been confirmed outside 19th-century Italy
They apply only to the distribution of agricultural land
They are fixed and hold identically in all fields observed
They are neither fixed nor universal, and vary greatly depending on the field
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry insists on this point: the numbers 80 and 20 are neither fixed nor universal, and even the proportion attributed to Pareto varies from one account to another; it is the disproportion that is general, not the number.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where is Vilfredo Pareto teaching in 1906, when he publishes his Manuale di economia politica?
choix: At the Academy of Sciences in Paris
At the University of Turin
At the University of Lausanne
In the parliament of the Kingdom of Italy, of which he is a member
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry indicates that in 1906 Pareto is still teaching at the University of Lausanne, where he has held the chair of political economy since 1893, when he publishes his Manuale di economia politica.
